1352.title: Open questions, kindly
1352.hook: Sikhs discuss the Ragmala, the calendar, diet and the Dasam Granth
1352.howItsDone: Sikhs discuss open questions such as the Ragmala, the calendar for gurpurabs, diet and the Dasam Granth in gurdwaras, homes and conferences, while the Rehat Maryada notes a difference of opinion on reading the Ragmala and asks that every copy of the Granth include it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh studies: lecture halls reading Gurbani and Sikh history closely. Your line was studied everywhere.

The program is over and the langar hall is emptying. At the end of one long row, two older men are still at it over steel cups of tea. One says the gurpurab dates should follow the old moon calendar, the way his grandfather kept them. The other says a fixed solar calendar makes more sense for Sikhs scattered across the world. Neither raises his voice. A teenager comes by with the kettle and fills both cups without being asked. The argument goes on, and so does the tea. Today opens a week of questions Sikhs are still talking about, and the way they hold them.
screen: `TWO MEN, ONE TABLE, ONE ARGUMENT.` → `THE KETTLE FILLS BOTH CUPS.` → `QUESTIONS STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: Sikhs name several questions out loud that the panth hasn't closed. Which calendar should set the dates of the gurpurabs. Whether an initiated Sikh may eat meat. Who wrote which parts of the Dasam Granth. And the Ragmala, a list of ragas at the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, which some Sikhs recite at the close of a full reading and others leave out. On that last one, the Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, doesn't pretend the matter is settled. Its readers point to a line that admits Sikhs hold differing opinions on reading the Ragmala, and then asks only that no copy of the Granth be written or printed without it. The question stays open. The book stays whole. That's a way of holding a disagreement: decide what you must, leave room where you can, and protect the thing everyone shares. On Ang 661, Guru Nanak says, here in paraphrase, that as long as we are in this world, we should listen to something and say something. Listening comes first in that line, and talk is part of a life of faith, not a failure of it. Sikhs have a word for this kind of thinking-through: vichar, reflection, turning a thing over carefully. Over the next days this path takes the questions one at a time: meat, the Dasam Granth, women among the five who serve amrit. It won't settle them. It will try to say each side the way its own people would.

Breathe in on that sentence and out on your own, and let both sit at the same table a while, like the two cups of tea; if you pray, rest on Waheguru while they sit there.

1353.title: The meat question
1353.hook: Sikhs hold different views on eating meat; the code forbids ritually slaughtered meat only
1353.howItsDone: Sikhs follow different diets: the Rehat Maryada forbids initiated Sikhs to eat kutha, ritually slaughtered meat; some Sikhs eat jhatka meat, others are vegetarian, and the langar is traditionally vegetarian so that all can share it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, open questions: the Ragmala, the calendar, and two cups of tea kept full during an argument. Your line was questions held kindly.

A family birthday, buffet style. Two cousins in line, both with a steel kara on the wrist, both wearing a turban. One fills a plate with dal, rice and paneer. The other adds a piece of tandoori chicken. Neither comments. An aunt watching from the end of the table has opinions, and keeps them for later. Ask Sikhs whether a Sikh can eat meat and the answers differ, sometimes inside one household. Today is that question, and what the Sikh code actually says.
screen: `TWO COUSINS, ONE BUFFET.` → `DAL ON ONE PLATE, CHICKEN ON ONE.` → `WHAT DOES THE CODE SAY?`

segments.voice: Start with the code; this path met its four things avoided back on day two hundred seventy. The Sikh Rehat Maryada lists a few things an initiated Sikh must never do. One is eating kutha, meat from an animal killed by ritual slaughter. Its readers notice what the line doesn't say: it doesn't forbid all meat. So some Sikhs eat meat killed with a single quick stroke, called jhatka, and see no conflict. Others read the whole spirit of Gurbani as pointing away from killing for food, and keep a vegetarian life. Some streams met earlier in this block, like the Namdharis, keep a vegetarian kitchen as a community. And the langar, the free kitchen, is traditionally vegetarian, so anyone of any diet can sit and eat the same meal. Now the Granth. In a passage on Ang 1289, Guru Nanak turns to people quarreling over flesh. In paraphrase: fools argue about meat, yet know nothing of spiritual wisdom or meditation. Readers hear that line in different ways. Some hear the Guru saying the argument itself misses the point. Others notice the passage goes on to observe that people are born of flesh, and read it as cutting through purity rules. Near the end of the Granth, couplets of Kabir speak sharply against killing, and some vegetarian Sikhs turn to them. So both sides open the same book. What they share is the line the code draws: no ritual slaughter, and a langar where every plate can be the same.

segments.voice: Think of one person whose plate looks different from yours, a vegetarian friend, a cousin who fasts, a coworker who keeps a rule you don't, and picture sitting across from them at one table. Let any small urge to comment go out with the breath, and think of one dish you could both share; if you pray, hold that table before Waheguru.
The meat question. Sikhs differ on eating meat; the code draws its line at ritually slaughtered meat, and the langar keeps one vegetarian table for all. Today's word.
Your line: different plates. The same book on both sides, and one langar for all. Until tomorrow.

1354.title: The Dasam Granth question
1354.hook: views differ on authorship of parts; devotion to Jaap and Chaupai is shared
1354.howItsDone: Sikhs differ on the authorship of parts of the Dasam Granth, while Jaap Sahib and Chaupai, which the Rehat Maryada places in the daily Nitnem, are recited morning and evening, and both are recited when amrit is prepared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meat question: no ritually slaughtered meat, and a langar where every plate can match. Your line was different plates.

A gutka is a small prayer book, wrapped in cloth, kept on a high shelf. Open one that has been used for years and the paper tells on its owner. Certain pages are softer than the rest, gray at the corners from thumbs, morning and evening. In some gutkas, two of those worn places are Jaap Sahib and Chaupai. Neither comes from the Guru Granth Sahib. Both come from another book, the Dasam Granth, and that book carries one of the open questions of the panth.
screen: `A SMALL BOOK ON A HIGH SHELF.` → `TWO WORN PLACES.` → `A SECOND GRANTH, A SECOND QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Dasam Granth means the book of the Tenth, the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh. It is a large collection: hymns of praise, long retellings of old stories, poetry about battle, and the Zafarnama, a letter to the emperor. Here the views differ. Some Sikhs hold that the whole collection is the Guru's own work. Others hold that parts of it, especially some of the long story sections, came from poets who gathered at his court. Others take a path between, accepting the prayers sung every day and studying the rest carefully. Scholars write books on it, and the conversation is sometimes heated. Now the part the sides share. Jaap Sahib is a cascade of short, rhythmic lines praising the Timeless One. It opens, here in paraphrase, by describing God as having no mark or sign, no color, no caste, no lineage. Chaupai is a prayer asking God's protection, plain and personal. The Sikh code of conduct places both among the daily prayers, the Nitnem: Jaap Sahib in the morning, Chaupai within the evening prayer. Both are recited when the amrit is prepared. So Sikhs who disagree sharply about the book's edges recite the same lines, morning and evening. A question about authorship doesn't have to empty the prayer. People can keep studying a hard question and keep their thumbs on the same worn page.
screen: `DASAM GRANTH: THE BOOK OF THE TENTH.` · `VIEWS DIFFER ON WHO WROTE WHICH PARTS.` · `JAAP AND CHAUPAI: IN THE DAILY PRAYERS.` · `STUDY THE QUESTION, KEEP THE PRAYER.` · then, large: `NO MARK, NO COLOR, NO CASTE.`

segments.voice: Bring up one question you carry that has no answer yet, about faith, family or what's true, and instead of gripping it, set it in an open palm; let your hand open on your knee if that helps. Breathe in and let the question stay, breathe out and let it stop demanding a verdict today, and if you pray, rest on the Timeless One whom Jaap Sahib praises.

1355.title: Women among the five
1355.hook: some gurdwaras include women among the Panj Pyare, some do not, and Sikhs discuss it
1355.howItsDone: At an amrit ceremony, five initiated Sikhs, the Panj Pyare, prepare and give amrit; some gurdwaras include women among the five, citing the Rehat Maryada and Gurbani, while others keep the five to men, following the first five.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dasam Granth question: views differ on who wrote parts of it, and Jaap Sahib and Chaupai are shared. Your line was shared devotion.

An amrit ceremony, in a closed room. Five initiated Sikhs in saffron stand around an iron bowl of water, stirring it with a double-edged khanda while they recite. They are the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones, standing in for the first five who answered the Guru's call. In one city, one of the five today is a woman. In another city, at another gurdwara, the five are always men. Both are Sikh ceremonies. Today is the conversation between them.
screen: `FIVE IN SAFFRON, ONE IRON BOWL.` → `IN ONE CITY, A WOMAN AMONG THEM.` → `IN ANOTHER, ALWAYS MEN.`

segments.voice: Begin with the story this path told on day eighty-four. Tradition says that at Anandpur, Guru Gobind Singh asked the gathered Sikhs who would give their head, and five men stepped forward one by one. They became the first Panj Pyare and received the first amrit. Tradition also says that Mata Sahib Kaur came and added sugar sweets to the water, so the amrit would carry sweetness along with the steel. So the first five were men, and a woman's hand is in the bowl. Here the views part. Some Sikhs hold that the five should follow the first five, and that the ceremony keeps its shape best by keeping its history. Others point to the Sikh code of conduct, whose readers say its section on the amrit ceremony allows Sikh women to be among the five. And they point to a line from the Asa di Var that this path met on the phulkari day. On Ang 473, Guru Nanak asks, here in paraphrase, why call her lesser, from whom kings are born? Here it's read as a question about who may stand at the bowl. In practice, some gurdwaras now include women among the Panj Pyare, and some do not. Both sides take the ceremony seriously, which is exactly why they care. The disagreement isn't about whether amrit matters. It's about how faithfully to keep a picture of the first day, and what faithfulness asks. Sikhs keep discussing it in gurdwara committees, in homes and online, and meanwhile the ceremony is held both ways.
screen: `FIVE MEN STEPPED FORWARD.` · `A WOMAN'S HAND IN THE BOWL.` · `THE CODE AND ANG 473.` · `TWO PRACTICES, ONE CEREMONY.` · then, large: `WHAT DOES FAITHFULNESS ASK?`

segments.voice: Think of a conversation in your own life that isn't finished, in your family, your work or your faith community, and don't try to win it or end it; just notice where it lives and whether it's still being held kindly. Then choose one small thing that would keep it open next time: a question, a pause, a cup of tea.

1356.title: Many voices
1356.hook: no single leader speaks for all Sikhs; the Granth and the sangat hold the panth together
1356.howItsDone: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as Guru and the Khalsa Panth as the community gathered around it; bodies like the Akal Takht and the Shiromani Committee carry weight, and local sangats run their own gurdwaras, but no single leader speaks for all Sikhs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, women among the five, and a ceremony held both ways. Your line was the conversation continues.

A reporter calls a gurdwara with a simple request. Can she speak to the head of the Sikh religion? The volunteer who picks up the phone pauses. There's a granthi who reads from the Granth here. There's a committee that runs the building. There's the Akal Takht in Amritsar, whose word carries real weight. But a single person who speaks for every Sikh on earth? The volunteer tries to explain, and the reporter keeps waiting for a name. Today is why there isn't one, and what holds the panth together instead.
screen: `CAN I SPEAK TO THE HEAD?` → `A GRANTHI, A COMMITTEE, A TAKHT.` → `BUT NO ONE VOICE.`

segments.voice: Sikh tradition says that before Guru Gobind Singh died, he ended the line of human Gurus. From then on, the Guru would be the Granth, the scripture, and the Khalsa Panth, the community of Sikhs gathered in the Guru's presence. Sikhs speak of Guru Granth and Guru Panth. That choice shapes everything this week has been about. There are respected bodies. The Akal Takht issues edicts, and they carry weight across the panth. The Shiromani Committee manages historic gurdwaras and published the code of conduct. Taksals and jathas have their own teachers. Local sangats run their own gurdwaras. But none of these is a single head over every Sikh. Authority is spread out, and it's meant to sit under the Granth, not over it. So how does a panth with many voices stay one? On Ang 72, Guru Nanak asks, here in paraphrase, how is the true congregation known? And answers: it is where the one Name is spoken. Not where one leader stands. Where the Name is. So a small sangat in a rented hall abroad, a great crowd at the Harmandir, and a family reading together at home can each be the sangat. Many voices is not a design flaw. It's what happens when the Guru is a book everyone can open, and the community is everyone who opens it. The voices sometimes clash. They also keep each other honest.

1357.title: One Granth for all
1357.hook: every stream bows to the same Guru Granth Sahib
1357.howItsDone: Across the Sikh streams the Guru Granth Sahib is installed under a canopy, read aloud and bowed to as Guru; Sikhs from any stream can follow the same hymns on the same pages in any gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many voices: no single head, and a true sangat known by the Name. Your line was many voices, one guru.

Go back over the streams this block has visited. A Nihang camp, blue robes and steel. An Udasi dera with its quiet ascetics. A Nirmala house of learning. A taksal where students drill every vowel. A Namdhari gathering in white. A sangat in New Mexico or Toronto singing in a mix of Punjabi and English. Different clothes, different tunes, different arguments. Now look at the front of each room. Raised a little, under a canopy, wrapped in cloth: the same book. Today is that book, at the center of the streams.
screen: `BLUE ROBES, WHITE CLOTHES, NEW TUNES.` → `LOOK AT THE FRONT OF THE ROOM.` → `THE SAME BOOK.`

segments.voice: The Guru Granth Sahib holds the hymns of Sikh Gurus alongside saints from other backgrounds, Kabir, Ravidas, Farid and more, gathered into one volume and sung in ragas. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh gave it the Guruship. Since then it is not treated as a book on a shelf: it is installed each morning under a canopy, read aloud, waved over with a whisk, and laid to rest at night. When one stream disagrees with another about diet, music, dress or the Dasam Granth, this is where both sides return. They bow to the same Guru. Gurbani gives the reason in Guru Ram Das's words on Ang 982, here in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word; within the Word are all the nectars. The Guru is not a person anyone can claim for their side. It is the Word itself, open on the same pages in every gurdwara. That has a practical effect. A Sikh walking into a gurdwara of a different stream, in another country, will find the same hymns and the same order of pages, and can sit down and follow along. The Namdharis, too, who keep a living guru of their own, bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and sing from it. The streams are many. The center is one book, and in each of those rooms, heads bow before it.

1358.title: Visiting another stream
1358.hook: all are welcome at any gurdwara; courtesy is enough
1358.howItsDone: Gurdwaras of every Sikh stream welcome visitors of any background; guests cover their heads, remove their shoes, leave tobacco and alcohol outside, sit on the floor facing the Guru Granth Sahib, receive karah prashad in cupped hands and may share langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Granth for all: every stream bows to the same Guru Granth Sahib. Your line was one granth.

A shoe rack by the door, already full. A basket of orange and blue head scarves for anyone who came without one. A small trough of water for washing hands. Nobody at the entrance asks which stream you belong to, or whether you're a Sikh at all. Someone may smile and point you toward the scarves. That's the whole admission process. This week has been full of questions Sikhs disagree about. It ends at the door every stream keeps open.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEAD COVERED, HANDS WASHED.` → `NOBODY ASKS WHICH STREAM.` → `A DOOR KEPT OPEN.`

segments.voice: Look back at the week: open questions held kindly, the meat question and its different plates, the Dasam Granth and its shared devotion, women among the five and a conversation that continues, many voices, and one Granth at the front of every room. What makes all that livable is this: any Sikh, and anyone else, can walk into a gurdwara of a stream not their own and be welcome. What's asked is courtesy, not agreement. Cover your head. Take off your shoes. Leave tobacco and alcohol outside. Sit on the floor with everyone else, facing the Granth, and don't turn your back to it or point your feet at it. If karah prashad, the warm sweet offering, is handed out, receive it in cupped hands. If you're invited to langar, sit in the row and eat what's served. No one checks your theology at the door. Gurbani gives a line for this openness. On Ang 671, Guru Arjan says, here in paraphrase, I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to all. A Nihang gurdwara may feel different from a Western sangat's, and a Namdhari gathering different again: the dress, the tunes, the pace. A visitor doesn't need to settle any of this week's questions to sit down. Courtesy is enough. Welcome does the rest.
screen: `A WEEK OF OPEN QUESTIONS.` · `COURTESY, NOT AGREEMENT.` · `HEAD, SHOES, FLOOR, CUPPED HANDS.` · `A FRIEND TO ALL.` · then, large: `COURTESY IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Picture a gurdwara you've never been to, or any place of worship you've wondered about, and walk through the visit in your mind: the shoes, the head covering, washing your hands, sitting down on the carpet. Notice any nervousness and let it out with the breath; if you pray, ask for an open heart on the way.
